name: Lɔɔma / Looma
confidence_why: Sadler (1949, published 2006), Dwyer (1981), Rude (1983), Vydrine (1989) and Mishchenko (2017) all describe Loma as a language with two level tones (high and low), lexical tone classes and tonal sandhi, none gives a word-stress rule, and Mishchenko (2017) states outright that Looma has no stress; the only tension is Sadler's passing remark that a second syllable 'receives more stress' after the definite suffix and Dwyer's general note that stress in Mande languages is non-contrastive, neither of which proposes a stress system for Loma.

catalog_quote: p. 85, Ch. V TONE: "5. There are two tones in Lɔɔma, high (´) and low (`). Low tone is marked only when it follows a high tone in the same word. ... When there is a series of low tones, only the first tone following the high tone is marked. ... High tone is marked wherever it occurs, except in a series of two or more high tones, in the same word, in wich case only the first high tone is marked. Compound words are toned as two separate words. ... Each word has its basic tones just as it has its basic consonants and vowels. Like the consonants and vowels, the tones undergo regular changes depending upon the environment. For example, the tone of a noun may be influenced by the tone class of the preceding possessive pronoun." || p. 20, sec. 1.7: "Tone. new_statements.rule_in_words: Looma is described as a two-tone (H/L) language with no word stress; the Liberian-specific handbook adds only that Lorma is syllable-timed (all syllables of equal duration) and gives a generic Mande/Kpelle stress rule (first H-toned syllable, else first syllable) without asserting it for Lorma. No Liberian Loma source opened states a word-stress position.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said in any source opened.
new_statements.exceptions: None as a rule; Sadler 1949/2006 p.21 incidentally notes that in taɣa-i 'the nest' 'the second syllable receives more stress' when the definite suffix -i is added (a one-word remark, not a system statement).
new_statements.domain_note: Mishchenko's statement is about the word-prosodic system (tone-bearing unit = syllable, toneme domain = morpheme/foot). Dwyer's remark concerns rhythm/timing at sentence level. Empirical base of the explicit 'no stress' statement is Guinean Woi-Balagha (toma1245), though the article's object language includes the Liberian dialects.
new_statements.first_reading: no word stress according to the source
new_statements.identity_note: The only explicit word-stress statement found (Mishchenko 2017, 'no stress') is from a whole-language encyclopedia article on Looma (Guinea + Liberia) whose data base is the Guinean Woi-Balagha dialect (= Glottolog toma1245, Toma); the article lists the Liberian dialects (Wubomai, Gbunde, Ziema, Briama, Zozo, Gizima) as part of its object language and does not flag stress as dialect-specific. The Liberian-specific descriptions opened (Sadler 1949/2006, Woozie, N. Liberia; Dwyer 1981a,b, Liberian Lorma/Gbunde; Vydrine 1989 after Sadler; Rude 1983, Zenalomai speaker) describe two tones and are silent on word stress except Dwyer's 'syllable-timed' note and Sadler's incidental remark.

new_statements.rule_in_words: No word-stress rule is given. Sadler treats Loma as a two-tone language (high vs. low, lexical tone classes A/B with tonal sandhi across words); Chapter I covers phonemes, vowel length, nasalisation, tone (cross-referenced to Ch. V) and syllable patterns but has no stress/accent section. The only use of the word 'stress' in the whole 109-page text is an incidental phonetic remark: in a-ɣ-a words that normally lose the velar fricative (taɣa > taa 'nest'), adding the definite suffix -i makes 'the second syllable receive more stress', which is why speakers keep the fricative (taɣai 'the nest'). This is a remark about one segmental alternation, not a statement of where word stress falls.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated for stress. The incidental remark concerns only definite-suffixed a-ɣ-a stems (sec. 1.10.1); compounds are toned as two separate words (p. 85).
new_statements.identity_note: Sadler's text was written in May 1949 at Woozie (Wozi), northern Liberia, and describes Liberian Loma (loma1260 proper). The existing catalog statement from Mishchenko 2017 draws its data from the Guinean Woi-Balagha dialect (toma1245, Toma), applied to Looma as a whole; Dwyer 1981 is Liberian Lorma.

readall_conflicts: No real disagreement. Sadler 2006 [1949], Dwyer 1981, Vydrine 1989, Rude 1983 and Mishchenko 2017 all describe Loma/Looma as a two-tone (H/L) language with tone classes and tonal sandhi, and none gives a word-stress placement rule. The only tension is soft: Mishchenko 2017 (Guinean Looma) states outright that stress is absent, while Sadler 2006 (Liberian Loma) never discusses stress but writes once, in passing, that after definite -i suffixation 'the second syllable receives more stress' (p. 21, sec. 1.10.1), which implies some phonetic prominence shift; it is an impressionistic 1949 remark used to explain why the velar fricative is retained in taɣai 'the nest', not a stress rule, and it does not amount to a claim of contrastive or fixed word stress. Dwyer 1981's Appendix E rule (stress on the first high-toned syllable, else the first syllable) is explicitly about Kpelle/Mande generally, not Lorma.
